overview: Balhae was founded in 698 by Dae Joyeong, a former Goguryeo general, in the hills of eastern Manchuria, and grew into a power that Tang writers called the Flourishing State of the East. Its capitals were laid out on the Tang model and its envoys sailed regularly to Japan.

items.text: Embassies went to Tang China and, more than thirty times, across the sea to Japan, carrying furs, ginseng and horses.
Balhae sat on the routes between Manchuria, the Korean peninsula, north China and the steppe.
Buddhism was practiced in the capitals, alongside the native beliefs of the Mohe majority.
A Tang-style government of three chancelleries and six ministries ran a state of many peoples; the capital Sanggyeong copied the grid of Chang'an.
Korea, China and Russia each claim Balhae's story in their national histories.
Excavations of its walled capitals and tombs show a state that mixed Goguryeo, Mohe and Tang traditions.

fall.text: The Khitan under Yelü Abaoji, founder of what became the Liao dynasty, took the capital Sanggyeong in 926 after a campaign of a few weeks. Refugees from the ruling class moved south into Goryeo.
